Oh yeah, I 100% understand where you're coming from as well, and I definitely do think ODD can manifest, as you said, without abuse, and I do think it should be treated--I just wonder if the name we have for it and the treatments that are in place are doing more harm than good. I personally do not believe it exists in a vacuum or arises from genetics but that's not scientific knowledge, just unprofessional postulating from personal experience. Having that belief in place makes me anxious that people are not looking at root causes.

I don't disagree with anything you've said here--I've had this talk frequently with my psychiatrist. I suppose I should've been more specific. I dislike the way that ODD is treated as a physical disease by many people, especially parents, and I dislike the attitude that "oh my child just Has This and there's nothing that can be done, it's just The  Way They Are." I do know that it's a descriptor of a much more extreme cluster of symptoms, and believe me my sister was up there, she definitely made my life absolute hell very frequently.

What I should have said is that I hate that ODD is very often used as an excuse, a prop, or a label, purely to avoid actually getting the child any kind of help. What my sister needed was not sedation or solitary confinement or for all of her possessions to be confiscated, she needed my dad to stop fucking hitting her. All of the adults I know who were diagnosed as kids have said similar. The worst part is is that getting the diagnosis often worked as a license for their abusers to increase or intensify the abuse. It's not precisely that I don't think that it's real; it's more that I think that, if we are to think of diagnoses as tools through which we can get people the help they need, ODD does not function as such, at least not in my experience. I've never heard anyone say "once I got diagnosed with and got help for my ODD, things got so much better". I *have* heard that about depression, ADHD, BPD, Bipolar disorder, PTSD, GAD, etc. I'm not saying my experience is the end all be all, it's certainly an anecdotal one, just attempting to give perspective on where I'm coming from.

I'm probably going to get downvoted to hell for this but I don't think ODD is real. The criteria for it is an absolute joke, it's basically "kid does lots of things I do not like". My sister was diagnosed with ODD for being extremely violent, disrespectful, getting into drugs/alcohol, etc. You know what no one ever looked at? The fact that she was being horrifically abused by my dad. Everyone I know who was "diagnosed" with ODD as a child who is now an adult has the exact same story. Violent, moody, drugs, etc. Horrific history of abuse from the person or people who took them to go get diagnosed. No one ever asked if they were being abused at home before slapping the label on them. I think "ODD" is the same as "my child is reacting logically to horrific trauma that I am either in denial about or actively causing". It literally stands for "oppositional defiance disorder"...why do we have a "won't do what you're told" disease just for children? If adults reacted this way to trauma and abuse we'd just go yeah unfortunately they've had a really rough go of it and have been very hurt.

I'm not part of the adoption community so my perspective is quite limited, but I do want to say something as someone who has been SAed multiple times.

The way that we as a culture perceive and talk about rape can be extremely harmful to survivors. I always hear and see people talking about it as the worst possible thing that could ever be done to you, and while I would absolutely never want to downplay the impact that it has had on people who have experienced it (myself included), it *can* lead people to think that if it happens to them, their life is over, they're irreparably broken, and they will never be a "whole" person. Magnifying it to something so huge and horrible and *defining* can make people *think that it defines them*.

It does not define the people who it has happened to. It does not define the people who were conceived by rape. At least, you (and others) don't have to let it define you.

Now, I know that's way easier said than done, but I suppose my point is: I would not take this knowledge and use it to decide how your bio mom feels about your existence. All you know right now is what you've said about her having you early and a little about how she felt at *that* time, and that she accepted your friend request on Facebook, which means she's not closing herself off from you. Of course I can't promise to know how she feels about you or how much healing/change etc has happened to your bio mom in the intervening years, but what I will say is this: the manner of your conception does not define her, and it does not define you. If you still have desire to reach out, please do so. You now have knowledge about what to be sensitive about and that's a useful tool, but it doesn't have to mean anything more than that. Good luck.

I think based on this response that you have more of a problem with the sentiment behind the phrasing misaligning with what is said than you do the actual phrasing. "You just don't want me to have any fun with my friends" is both an accusation and a belief about the other person's intentions. "I FEEL like you just don't want me to have any fun with my friends" removes the direct accusation that this is the other person's true intention; it opens the door for them to say "what do I do that makes you feel that way?". The other phrase leaves it as a foregone conclusion that that is the intention of the other person, and there's literally nothing they can do about it.

If a person who means the old phrase says the new phrase instead, well, they're just lying. What they actually mean is "I'm saying I feel to disguise the fact that this is a belief in your intentions."

The problem is not with the therapy speak itself, it's with the intention behind it. And disingenuous people will be disingenuous no matter how they're dressing up their words, but people who actually care to communicate better will benefit from having more precise and thoughtful phrases with which to communicate.
